reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and triple assessment guidance
clinicalPearls: A fibroadenoma is the commonest benign solid breast lump in young women, typically presenting in the late teens to early thirties
It classically feels smooth, firm, rounded, and highly mobile within the breast, earning the nickname breast mouse
It is usually painless and slow-growing, and may be found incidentally or during breast self-awareness
Diagnosis follows the principle of triple assessment, combining clinical examination, imaging, and needle biopsy where indicated
In women under about twenty-five with typical features and concordant imaging, tissue diagnosis may not always be required, but any diagnostic uncertainty warrants biopsy
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice in young women, typically showing a well-defined, oval, hypoechoic mass, with mammography reserved for older patients
Once benign diagnosis is confirmed, small asymptomatic fibroadenomas can be safely observed, with excision considered for large, enlarging, symptomatic, or patient-preference cases
A rapidly enlarging fibroadenoma-like mass, especially in an older woman, should raise the possibility of a phyllodes tumour and prompt further assessment
reference.pathophysiology: A fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic tumour arising from the terminal duct lobular unit, in which both the glandular epithelium and the surrounding specialised stroma proliferate. It is regarded as an aberration of normal breast development rather than a true neoplasm, and its growth is influenced by oestrogen, which is why fibroadenomas typically appear during the reproductive years, may enlarge in pregnancy, and tend to involute after the menopause. The well-circumscribed, encapsulated architecture gives the characteristic smooth, freely mobile clinical lump. Malignant change within a fibroadenoma is very rare.
additionalDifferentials: Fibrocystic change with a dominant lump
additionalInvestigations: Clinical breast examination as part of triple assessment
Ultrasound as first-line imaging in young women
Mammography in women over the appropriate age threshold or with atypical features
Core needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis where imaging or clinical features are not classically benign
Fine-needle aspiration cytology in selected settings
Interval imaging follow-up when a lesion is observed rather than excised
redFlags: Rapid enlargement suggesting a phyllodes tumour
Irregular, hard, or fixed mass or associated skin or nipple changes
Discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathological findings on triple assessment
A new discrete solid lump in an older woman that must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise
reference.prognosis: Fibroadenomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; many remain stable or regress over time, recurrence after complete excision is uncommon, and the associated increase in future breast cancer risk is minimal except in the uncommon complex subtype.
pitfalls: Assuming any young woman's lump is a fibroadenoma without completing triple assessment
Missing a phyllodes tumour presenting as a rapidly growing fibroadenoma-like mass
Failing to biopsy a solid lump in an older woman where malignancy is more likely
Over-treating small, asymptomatic, confirmed benign lesions with surgery
references: Standard breast surgery reference text on benign breast disease
Guidance on triple assessment of breast lumps
management: Confirm the benign diagnosis through triple assessment combining clinical examination, ultrasound and core needle biopsy where indicated
Reassure and offer conservative management with interval clinical and ultrasound follow-up for small, asymptomatic, typical fibroadenomas
Offer surgical excision for large, enlarging or symptomatic lesions, diagnostic uncertainty or patient preference
Consider minimally invasive options such as vacuum-assisted excision or cryoablation as alternatives to open surgery in suitable cases
Biopsy any lesion with atypical or discordant imaging, and follow complex fibroadenomas more closely given their small associated risk
Refer to a breast clinic for assessment of any new or changing breast lump
